title: pascal: the quiet room
hookLine: Pascal: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber (Pensées 139, Trotter's 1910 translation)

lines: A PLAIN ROOM. NOTHING TO DO.
cards: Try this, just in your head. You're in a plain room. No phone.
No book. Nobody else. Nothing to do for fifteen minutes.

How long before you reach for something? Researchers at the University of Virginia tried a version of this in 2014. They left people alone with nothing but their thoughts and a button that gave a mild electric shock.
People who had already tried the shock, and said they'd pay to avoid it, still pushed the button: most of the men, and about a quarter of the women. Anything, rather than just sitting.

teach.h: THE POSTER LINE IS A PARAPHRASE.
teach.b: His name was Blaise Pascal. As a young man he built one of the first mechanical calculators and did serious work on probability.

Later, after an intense religious experience, he filled his last years with notes toward a defense of Christian faith. He died at thirty-nine, and his friends published the notes as the Pensées, the thoughts.
You may have seen one on a poster: all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone. That's a modern paraphrase.

An old English translation has it this way: "I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." Not problems. Unhappiness.
A man will chase a hare all day, Pascal says, that he wouldn't take if you handed it to him. He doesn't want the hare. He wants the chase, because it keeps him from thinking about himself.
Pascal's own answer to what waits in the quiet room was a Christian one. But his observation stands by itself: the restlessness isn't a sign something is wrong with you. He saw it in everyone.
Zen Buddhism in Japan built a whole practice around sitting, called zazen.
The teacher Dogen taught a form called shikantaza, just sitting: no goal, nothing to win.
You sit, and the restlessness comes and goes like anything else. Two very different reasons. Both noticed the chair.

how: Many traditions have a practice of simply sitting still: Zen Buddhists sit zazen, often facing a wall; Quakers gather in silent worship; and many people keep a few quiet minutes alone at the start or end of the day.

games.q: who said what, and what it means — tap the pairs.
p: thoughts: notes published after he died

s: Pascal wrote "all of humanity's problems stem from…"
that's a modern paraphrase. Trotter's 1910 translation says "all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact."
in a 2014 study, many people chose a mild shock over sitting alone with their thoughts
most of the men and about a quarter of the women pushed the button.
feeling restless when you sit means you're doing it wrong
Pascal saw the restlessness in everyone. in Zen's just sitting, it comes and goes like anything else.

games.q: Pascal describes a man chasing a hare all day, a hare he wouldn't take if you handed it to him. why does he chase it?
o: the chase keeps him from thinking about himself.
he wants to prove he's brave.
games.why: for Pascal, it's the chase, not the hare. the busyness keeps us from the quiet room.

practice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Let your hands rest in your lap.
Sit. Breathe. Notice the small pull to do something else.
You don't have to fight it, and you don't have to obey it. That pull is exactly what Pascal was writing about, and you're sitting with it.

wordCard.voice: Sit. The simplest instruction there is, and somehow one of the hardest. Not to do anything. Just to stay. Tenth word.

orig.note: Japanese, from Zen Buddhism: za, sitting; zen, meditation. the seated practice at the heart of Zen.

carryVoice: Your line: sit anyway. A restless sit still counts as a sit, every time. Day ten.
